title: Why Teachers Play Multiple Roles
brief: Introduce the central idea that a teacher is not a single fixed presence but shifts between several distinct roles depending on what the lesson demands at any given moment. Draw on the module's repeated framing of teacher-centered versus student-centered lessons and its questions about when teachers should step back to let students produce language or lead discussion. Use the module's contrast between lessons where the teacher speaks almost exclusively (target language use throughout) and moments where students are invited to take over (student-led discussion activities, peer assessment) to show why role-switching matters. Close by listing the six roles—controller, organizer, monitor, prompter, facilitator, resource—that the rest of the unit will examine one by one.

title: Controller and Organizer: Leading from the Front
brief: Explain the controller role by drawing on source moments where the teacher directs every element of the lesson: greeting latecomers, giving instructions, managing off-task students who stand when they should sit or talk out of turn, and keeping the lesson on track when students make off-topic comments. Show the organizer role through the module's descriptions of smooth transitions between activities, assigning students to groups, and sequencing activities from opening movement warm-ups through vocabulary presentation to wrap-up. Use the module's observation that some lessons are explicitly teacher-centered to illustrate when these two roles are most active, and note that heavy use of controller and organizer roles limits student output—a tension the unit will return to.

title: Monitor: Watching Without Interrupting
brief: Define the monitor role as the teacher circulating and observing student performance without taking over, and anchor this in the module's discussion of how teachers check comprehension informally through student performance during activities rather than through formal tests. Draw on the module's questions about how teachers evaluate whether lesson objectives were met—formally or informally—and its examples of teachers watching students during TPR activities and games such as Hot Potato to gauge understanding. Emphasize the module's point that monitoring must not disrupt the flow of the lesson, illustrated by the repeated guidance on managing off-task students without breaking lesson momentum. Distinguish monitoring from controlling: the teacher is present and attentive but is not directing.

title: Prompter and Resource: Supporting Without Taking Over
brief: Explain the prompter role using the module's examples of teachers responding when students give no answer or an incorrect answer—laughing and smiling rather than scolding, providing encouragement and positive reinforcement, and using elicitation techniques to draw out student responses rather than simply supplying the answer. Introduce the resource role through the module's depictions of teachers using puppets, audio materials, realia, and graphic organizers as tools students can consult, and through the Discussion Leader and Peer Assessment worksheets that give students structured support for leading their own discussions. Stress that both roles involve the teacher offering just enough help to keep students moving forward while leaving the cognitive work with the learner.

title: Facilitator: Stepping Back So Students Do the Work
brief: Present the facilitator role as the point at which the teacher most deliberately reduces their own presence so that students take responsibility for learning. Use the module's explicit contrast between teacher-centered and student-centered lessons, its questions about how to make a teacher-centered lesson more student-centered, and its examples of student-led discussion activities supported by self-assessment and peer assessment rubrics. Draw on the module's observation that students in some lessons had limited opportunities to freely produce language, and its suggestions for activities that enable more student output, to show what facilitation looks like in practice. Include the module's example of a teacher choosing to extend discussion time when students are engaged as a concrete moment of facilitation—the teacher reads the room and gets out of the way.

title: Knowing When to Switch: Reading the Lesson
brief: Bring the roles together by focusing on the decision-making process: how does a teacher know which role to adopt at a given moment? Use the module's lesson structure—opening warm-up, vocabulary presentation, practice activities, wrap-up—to show how different phases naturally call for different roles, with the controller and organizer most active at the start, the monitor and prompter active during practice, and the facilitator most visible when students are engaged in extended tasks. Draw on the module's recurring questions about timing (extending activities when students are engaged, keeping students on task, ending with movement) to illustrate that switching roles is a response to what is actually happening in the classroom. Close by returning to the module's framing of reflecting and adapting: teachers should consider what went well and what they might do differently, treating role choice as something to review and refine after every lesson.
